This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a random parking function generated from the uniform distribution, specifically focusing on the asymptotic behavior of its initial positions as the available spots and inputs both increase with a uniform distribution. It demonstrates that given the sequence of first $k$ positions, the sequence of remaining elements is statistically equivalent to a random sample from the set of unused elements, drawn from a uniform distribution. Furthermore, the paper establishes that the first $k$ positions, when properly scaled, follow the same uniform discrete distribution as the standard parking function. Moreover, the paper shows that the difference between the standard and uniform discrete distributions diminishes exponentially with the size of the set.

Researchers have long debated the origins of conductance loss in superconducting nanowires, with two primary theories being the coherent quantum phase-slip and the Coulomb blockade. To resolve this dispute, we conducted a series of experiments on NbN nanowires, with their conductance modulated by an external gate electrode. Our measurements revealed a hysteresis effect in the gate voltage that vanished below a critical temperature, indicating the dominance of quantum phase-slips. Furthermore, the critical current exhibited characteristics of coherent behavior, with an increase in sample size leading to an increase in critical current. Our study provides conclusive evidence in favor of the quantum quantum phase-slip model over the Coulomb blockade model.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 was a significant milestone in astronomy, as it was initially thought to be a low-mass brown dwarf, but its mass was later found to be significantly higher than expected, given its high temperature. This discrepancy has been a longstanding puzzle in astronomy, and in this study, we aim to shed light on it by using advanced spectroscopic analysis techniques to determine the chemical composition of GJ 229B. Our analysis reveals that the object's atmosphere is heavily depleted in lithium, and that its chemical composition is consistent with that of a low-mass star, rather than a brown dwarf. This finding suggests that GJ 229B may in fact be a low-mass star, and that its high mass estimate may be due to inaccuracies in its radial velocity measurements. Our results also provide a new constraint on the object's luminosity, and suggest that it may be more luminous than previously estimated. This study highlights the importance of accurate spectroscopic analysis in determining the chemical composition of low-mass objects, and that further research is needed to fully understand the nature of GJ 229B.

Our study utilizes state-of-the-art simulations of gluon plasma, generated through the case-by-case method, to investigate deep inelastic scattering off quark-gluon plasma. By incorporating the Weizsacker-Williams approximation, we can extract the virtual boson's structure function from scattering data. Our analysis shows that the scattering process can effectively probe the internal properties of the simulated plasma, revealing characteristic features of its complex structure. The results are presented in a visual format, illustrating the virtual boson's structure function across a range of momentum transfer values. The data is compared to the theoretical predictions of parton distribution functions for a quark-gluon plasma, highlighting the distinct features of this unique state of matter. The study also discusses the implications of our findings for understanding the properties of the quark-gluon plasma and the potential for further research in this area. The research was supported by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

To create a novel view video from a single input video, our approach leverages a dual representation that combines a 3D scene model with a 2D image features map. This method enables us to generate videos from novel viewpoints by rendering the 3D scene model and blending it with the original image features. Our technique is straightforward to implement and can be trained using any dataset that provides video clips from multiple viewpoints of the same scene. Notably, our method outperforms existing learning-based approaches in terms of visual realism and temporal consistency.

In this study, we present inter-orbital coupling in a Bose-Einstein condensate, achieved by superimposing two distinct orbital modes in a double-loop trap. A Sagnac interferometer is employed to create this interference between the modes, and we observe oscillations in the major axis of the condensate's inertia when subjected to weak rotation. Our findings indicate that coupling orbitals can enhance the sensitivity of atom interferometers and improve the coherence of atomic systems.

The $\Omega^{-}$ baryon, which contains one s-quark, is a crucial target for LHCb to reach the Full Physics Run at the LHC. By utilizing LHCb's excellent flavor tagging and mass resolution, we can search for the long-predicted Strangeness=-3 $\Omega^{-}$ baryon. Utilizing $K^+K^+K^-p$ final states, we analyze data collected by LHCb from 2011 to 2018. With an integrated luminosity of 5.0 fb$^{-1}$, 900 pb$^{-1}$, and 9.8 fb$^{-1}$, no $\Omega^{-}$ baryons were found, and at a 95% confidence level, the upper limit on its production cross-section multiplied by detection efficiency is set at 11.3 pb, 4.14 pb, and 10.9 pb for respective runs. These limits surpass previous theoretical and experimental estimates.

Enclosed spaces with high occupant turnover rates, such as public transit, pose significant risks for disease transmission. While the ventilation system's role in airborne disease spread is acknowledged, the specific mechanisms at play are not fully understood. To investigate this, we used a well-mixed model to analyze the spread of an airborne virus on a single bus in New York City. By analyzing the ventilation system and applying statistical methods to survey data, we were able to estimate the transmission risk. Our analysis revealed that the risk is primarily influenced by the number of infected and uninfected individuals on the bus, as well as the ventilation system's ability to remove airborne viruses. The risk was found to be low in most cases, but increased significantly when an infected individual boarded a bus with poor ventilation. The model developed in this study can be used to design ventilation systems that minimize the spread of airborne diseases in urban buses.

Building on recent findings, our calculations offer a more precise detection method for quantum vacuum effects such as birefringence and light deflection during high-energy photon interactions with other photons. To achieve this enhanced detection, we suggest utilizing the distinctive polarization patterns produced in the process, specifically by analyzing the relationship between the initial and final light's polarization states. Furthermore, our proposed detection method involves comparing the probability of this process with the standard process of birefringence, which can be measured through conventional laboratory experiments.

This note outlines the algorithm developed by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space.

Broadbent, Lord, and Schaffner first introduced the concept of quantum unclonable encryption in 2017, a novel primitive that addresses the limitations of classical unclonable encryption and has no direct quantum counterpart. This scheme leverages the unique properties of quantum mechanics to achieve security beyond what's possible classically. Specifically, it allows for the creation of an unbreakable encryption method that can only be decrypted by a single authorized party. This research revisits and re-examines the initial construction and security proofs of quantum unclonable encryption presented by Broadbent, Lord, and Schaffner. The new proof is simpler and more straightforward than the original, while also providing a streamlined demonstration of how the initial construction can be improved to use smaller, more manageable quantum states. The new security proof shows that the scheme remains secure even when using smaller states of $O(n^{3/2})$ qubits, compared to the initial construction's $O(n^2)$ qubits. This research has significant implications for the development of secure quantum communication protocols and may pave the way for the creation of new, innovative quantum communication technologies.

This study develops a physical-layer authentication protocol for Gaussian noise channels that utilizes shared secrets, bypassing the need for cryptographic keys.
We utilize binary patterns that are naturally generated by a communication device's hardware and preserved through transmission to a receiving device as unique identifiers.
To verify the identity of a transmitting device, the patterns are compared with previously recorded ones, allowing for a balance between false acceptance and unique device identification.
Optimal patterns are determined through a new cost function that minimizes verification errors, and efficient algorithms are proposed for accurate and low-complexity detection.
Simulation results indicate that a successful verification requires a minimum of 1000 bits and a verification accuracy of 99.999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999

We have performed first-principles calculations to investigate the flat-band plasmons in twisted bilayer MoS$_2$. Our analysis shows that plasmons within the flat bands are highly localized, with minimal interlayer mixing, and can be described by separate descriptions for each layer. The plasma frequency of these plasmons is influenced by the twist angle, and can be attributed to variations in the flat-band width, and can be understood through an effective mass approximation. The frequency can be increased by applying an electric field to separate the layers, and the plasmons within the flat bands are more confined than those in twisted monolayer graphene.

This research paper establishes the structure equation for an almost conformal Ricci soliton when placed on a Sasakian manifold and analyzes its features in this context. Additionally, we demonstrate that a conformal Ricci soliton on a shrinking Ricci soliton that is defined over a Kenmotsu solvmanifold must have its potential function be a linear function. Furthermore, we provide a demonstration that a conformal Ricci soliton that is defined over a Sasakian space form with a scalar curvature of 1 can be considered as a Ricci soliton that is defined over the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}$.

This lecture will discuss the connections between stellar winds, magnetic fields, and exoplanetary systems. We will examine how magnetic fields in young stars interact with their accretion processes and how these factors affect star-planet systems. Additionally, we will analyze extreme cases of star-planet systems, specifically hot Jupiters, to understand how magnetic fields in these systems influence their dynamics.

The spin-orbit proximity effect (SPCE) is a phenomenon that occurs when a thin metallic layer is in contact with a strong spin-orbit material, leading to the transfer of spin-orbit interactions to the metal. This effect is being investigated in a high-quality molybdenum dicobalt (Mo/Co) multilayer, where the Mo layers are just a single atomic layer thick. Due to the large spin-orbit coupling in Mo, the Heisenberg exchange and the induced spin-orbit interactions in the Co layers can be examined. Our study reveals that the strength of the induced spin-orbit coupling in the Co layers is significantly influenced by the quality of the interface between Mo and Co. In samples with sharp interfaces, the induced spin-orbit coupling is found to be in good agreement with theoretical predictions, whereas in samples with diffuse interfaces, the induced spin-orbit coupling is much weaker. These results can be explained by the fact that the Mo/Co interface is not uniform, and only a small fraction of the Mo/Co interface exhibits strong spin-orbit coupling. Our research provides valuable insights into the control of the SPCE through the modulation of the weak interface scattering.

This research focuses on solving the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation for a generalized Mie-type potential in multiple dimensions, utilizing the Jumarie type fractional derivative. Analytical expressions for this potential were derived using a specific transformation, and the application of the variational iteration method enabled us to obtain approximate solutions for the associated wave function. Furthermore, graphical representations of the obtained solutions were generated to visualize the behavior of the wave function.

We investigate the impact of a neural network's sensitivity to input changes on its performance, and demonstrate that limiting its sensitivity can significantly improve its ability to generalize. To achieve this, we introduce a new optimization method that penalizes a neural network's Lipschitz constant, and prove that this approach guarantees optimal convergence. We also show that this technique can be applied to various optimization measures, and that it is particularly effective when used to regularize overfitting in neural networks. Our experiments with both synthetic data and real-world image classification tasks reveal that our method produces networks with lower Lipschitz constants and superior classification accuracy, and that it is capable of generating more robust networks that are less susceptible to adversarial attacks.

Sequential neural networks have achieved significant success in various natural language processing tasks, particularly in the area of part-of-speech tagging. These models excel at making predictions based on contextual information, but their performance suffers when dealing with the non-sequential phenomenon of agreement. To investigate whether these models can learn to process agreement, we focused on the Basque language and conducted an experiment using the ETLB corpus. Our results indicate that while sequential neural networks can make accurate predictions, they do not truly capture the phenomenon of agreement. Instead, they rely on a non-sequential strategy of looking ahead for the agreeing element, which is not always available in the input sequence. This suggests that part-of-speech tagging models need to be designed to process long-distance dependencies more efficiently.

HD 80606 b is a unique exoplanet that offers valuable insights into how planetary formation processes can lead to diverse outcomes. Its highly eccentric orbit and substantial mass, which is comparable to that of a brown dwarf, are the result of an unusual formation process. Researchers believe that this planet may have formed in close proximity to its star and migrated inward over time. To better understand and predict the planet's orbit, scientists are using data from the Keck and VLT telescopes to observe the star's movements. These observations will help refine our knowledge of HD 80606's position in the sky and pave the way for future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope. By analyzing the data collected from these observations, the team aims to improve their understanding of the planet's orbit and identify the most efficient times to observe it with the JWST.

The use of video games in therapy has been shown to be effective in improving motor skills and engagement in rehabilitation. To enhance the design of therapeutic games, researchers are combining data-driven modeling with traditional design methods. By employing gameplay metrics and clustering techniques, they are developing a comprehensive understanding of how players interact with a virtual reality climbing game, which can inform the development of more effective treatment programs. The resulting analysis provides a foundation for designers to create engaging and beneficial gaming experiences for patients undergoing rehabilitation.

Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both non-cohesive and cohesive materials.

We investigate the impact of vector leptoquarks on the Drell-Yan process, specifically in the context of a Standard Model extension that includes two types of leptoquarks with lepton number -1 and -2. The impact of these new particles is most noticeable in the lepton pair invariant mass spectrum at high masses. To accurately describe this, we use a next-to-leading order QCD calculation for the Drell-Yan process, supplemented by precision predictions for the top quark contribution. The implementation of these models in the MatchMC generator is also presented, which allows for a precise comparison with experimental data from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations. The results indicate that the presence of vector leptoquarks can be constrained by the top quark contribution, but not significantly by the Drell-Yan process.

Deep learning-based reconstruction methods for PET imaging have achieved high-quality results, but increasing computational costs and a lack of interpretability pose challenges. These techniques struggle to process lower-dose data, which contains a high level of noise. This paper introduces a new approach for lower-dose PET imaging that utilizes uncertainty-aware neural networks guided by physics principles and incorporates an uncertainty-based mixture of experts framework. This model leverages input data and a reference scan to generate a high-dose PET image, while a probabilistic neural network outputs uncertainty maps to guide learning and mitigate the effects of high noise levels. A novel loss function is proposed to enhance robustness in the presence of low-signal data. Experimental results on a Siemens Prisma PET/MR scanner demonstrate the proposed method's ability to produce high-dose PET images with reduced artifacts and a more accurate uncertainty estimation compared to existing techniques.

The concept of personalization has gained significant popularity in recent years, with numerous companies investing in technologies designed to tailor user experiences. However, these advancements come with a caveat: they often require compromising user privacy. As the line between personalization and privacy continues to blur, it becomes increasingly important for us to educate our students on the distinction and the role they can play in safeguarding their own privacy. This presentation aims to engage students in a discussion about the balance between personalization and privacy, and to inspire them to take an active role in protecting their own data.

The centering theory, a prominent discourse analysis framework, posits that linguistic elements are linked to discourse structure through the mechanism of "forward and backward looking." This study aims to assess the applicability of centering theory within the context of neural coreference resolution systems. To accomplish this, we have developed a specialized dataset comprising sentences annotated with centering-relevant features, which are then employed to train and test models for predicting coreferential relationships. The findings reveal that while the influence of sentence context on coreference resolution aligns with centering theory's principles, the magnitude of this effect is minimal. The study's outcome suggests that centering theory may play a limited role in guiding the decision-making process of state-of-the-art neural coreference resolution models.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

The performance of a computer system is heavily influenced by its configuration, 
which can be altered through various methods such as adjusting the BIOS settings, 
modifying the operating system parameters, and customizing applications. 
However, manually configuring a system to achieve peak performance is a time-consuming 
and complex task. To address this challenge, automated configuration techniques have 
been developed, but they are often limited to specific aspects of system configuration 
and require human intervention to create initial configurations. Our research proposes 
a unified framework for automated system configuration that encompasses both binary and 
continuous configuration variables, covers multiple software and hardware components, 
and allows for the creation of configurations through a combination of optimization 
and machine learning methods. We have developed three modules within this framework: 
AutoConfig, which generates configurations using a combination of machine learning and 
optimization techniques, AutoCompose, which combines configurations from different 
software and hardware components, and AutoTune, which refines configurations through 
automated parameter tuning. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our framework 
by developing an automated configuration strategy for a combination of a CPU, SSD, 
database server, and web server, resulting in a configuration that outperforms both 
default and hand-tuned configurations.

We introduce a method to study the spatial distribution of operators that develop in time, specifically focusing on their ability to be recreated locally. This approach is applied to various models, including free bosons and fermions, as well as interacting bosons and fermions. Our research reveals that in models with nonspreading dynamics, there exists an intricate entanglement between the initial state and the time factor in the operator, which can be recreated locally. Conversely, in chaotic systems, the operator's growth is driven by the time component, and the entanglement with the initial state is minimal. This distinction can be leveraged to design experiments that differentiate between different types of time evolution. Furthermore, our study shows that strong interactions between particles can be detected through the analysis of the operator's entanglement.

As the use of wireless local area networks grows, accurately determining distances between devices without physical markers becomes increasingly challenging. This task is complicated by the unreliable nature of WiFi signals, which are influenced by various environmental factors. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of multiple regression techniques for estimating distances based on received signal strength, considering the noise characteristics of the data. Our analysis shows that the choice of regression model significantly impacts estimation accuracy, with the optimal model varying depending on the specific data set. Our research also provides a means for selecting the most suitable machine learning approach for this application.

A highly advanced civilization living on a planet orbiting a star would face a unique challenge when their star eventually becomes a black hole.  Normally, such a star would become a red giant, engulfing the planet and destroying it.  However, if this civilization had already mastered the technology to harness energy from their star, they could potentially adapt their infrastructure to extract energy from the black hole instead.  Using the Penrose process, they could tap into the rotational energy of the black hole, as long as it was spinning.  Although this process is less efficient than direct solar energy collection, it could still provide a sustainable energy source.  As a result, this civilization would construct a Dyson sphere around the former star, now using it in conjunction with the black hole to power their world.

A critical aspect of providing reliable web services is ensuring they meet agreed-upon quality standards. To achieve this, organizations rely on monitoring systems that can detect and address any deviations from these standards. However, these systems can be compromised by inaccurate or manipulated monitoring data. To counter this, we propose incorporating peer-to-peer technology into the monitoring system. By enabling independent verification of monitoring data by third-party nodes, we can more accurately detect deviations from service level agreements. Our approach leverages a decentralized system to minimize the impact of compromised nodes and reduce the latency in detecting violations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution through a prototype implementation and performance evaluation.

The beam breakup instability in energy recovery linacs poses a significant threat to the stable operation of the machine, particularly when dealing with high beam power. To address this issue, understanding how different filling patterns within a train affect beam breakup instability is crucial. This study investigates the impact of filling patterns on longitudinal and transverse beam breakup instability by analyzing the growth rate and mode number of unstable modes. Our research reveals that both types of instability are heavily influenced by filling patterns, with the mode number of unstable modes varying significantly. Specifically, the mode number of unstable modes is determined by the number of empty linacs in the train, with a direct relationship between the two. This study also derives a general formula for calculating the growth rate of unstable modes, which can be applied to any arbitrary filling pattern. The results obtained in this study are presented in a tabular format, providing a comprehensive overview of the relationship between filling patterns and beam breakup instability.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of neutron interaction processes based on total cross-section data obtained from neutron detection rates using a specialized 3D-projection scintillator detector. The detector's design incorporates 120 individual 3D-projection units, each consisting of 100 thin CH foils and a 10-inch photomultiplier tube, enabling the measurement of neutron flux at various depths within the detector. The novel 3D-projection detector design facilitates the determination of total cross-section data by comparing the relative neutron detection rates at different CH depths, thereby circumventing the need for absolute detection rate measurements. The cross-section data obtained from this study align closely with established measurements from other experiments and theoretical predictions, validating the 3D-projection detector's effectiveness for neutron detection and demonstrating its suitability for use in neutron imaging applications.

The initial growth of planetary bodies relies heavily on sticking properties in particle ensembles influenced by electrostatic forces. To better understand how temperatures in protoplanetary discs affect these sticking properties, experiments were conducted on various particle ensembles under different temperature conditions. The experiments covered a range of temperatures from 293K to 423K, simulating the changes in a protoplanetary disc. The results showed that the critical charge required for sticking decreases as temperatures increase, which could be explained by the reduction in relative humidity. The critical charge also remains proportional to the square root of particle radius, which is consistent with theoretical predictions. The findings suggest that the growth of planetary bodies may be limited by the sticking properties in warmer regions of a protoplanetary disc, which could be explained by the reduction in relative humidity. The implications of this study on the formation of planetary bodies in various types of protoplanetary discs are discussed.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely utilized for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies, including basic, kernel-based, and different weighting strategies, and visualize the results effectively. This package is particularly useful for data sets with nonlinear structures, and can be found at the CRAN repository.

Imitation learning has been extensively studied in robotics, with the focus primarily on learning from demonstrations. However, real-world applications require robots to adapt to novel situations, navigate through complex environments, and adhere to nonlinear hard constraints. This research presents a comprehensive imitation learning framework that encompasses adaptation, nonlinear hard constraints, and obstacle avoidance. The proposed framework utilizes an optimal control approach to learn from demonstrations, with a policy that can adapt to new conditions, avoid obstacles, and satisfy nonlinear hard constraints. The framework is evaluated on multiple robotic tasks, with promising results indicating its ability to learn from demonstrations, adapt to novel situations, navigate through complex environments, and adhere to nonlinear hard constraints.

Using the BFKL formalism, a one-loop central-emission vertex for two gluons has been calculated in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory, yielding a result of -0.632764 for a specific parameter value. A direct numerical integration method was employed to verify this calculation. A relationship between this integral and the Euler gamma constant was derived, providing a more efficient method for obtaining this value. A comparison was made with a previously published result using a different integration method, which initially yielded an incorrect value of -0.466021 due to a numerical error. A central-emission diagram was also visualized for the process being studied.

A novel phase of superconductivity, dubbed spin-singlet topological superconductivity (SS-STS), has been found in a two-dimensional Rashba model with an attractive interaction. This phase, which emerges in the presence of a minimum chemical potential, is characterized by a non-zero superconducting gap and a non-trivial topological invariant. The discovery of this phase is made possible by a unique interplay between the Rashba effect and a specific type of pairing symmetry. The phase is marked by the coexistence of spin-orbit coupling and topological invariant, which results in the appearance of Majorana zero modes at the system's edges. The discovery of this phase is of great interest due to its potential applications in topological quantum computing.

The behavior of vortices in superconductors when exposed to magnetic fields is a key area of study, and understanding this can lead to improved superconducting materials. In this study, we used a technique called third-harmonic AC susceptibility to observe the movement of vortices in a high-temperature superconductor, YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.95}$, as we gradually increased the magnetic field. We observed a distinct change in the movement of vortices, and through analysis, determined that this change occurred at a critical point. We also determined the critical parameters of this transition and found that it aligns with the movement of a first-order phase transition. We then attempted to visualize the lattice of vortices and found that it takes on a square-square shape at a critical point, and this can be explained by a specific theoretical model.

Theories of molten polymer brushes have been extensively studied, yet they have been limited to statically stretched brushes. New research has now expanded these theories to encompass dynamically stretched brushes, which can occur when a substrate with attached polymers undergoes rapid deformation. Calculated force-extension relationships for this new scenario have been derived for various shapes, including curved surfaces and stretched molten brushes on flat substrates. Notably, force-extension relationships for dynamically stretched brushes exhibit a unique feature: an "exclusion zone" that vanishes as the stretching rate increases beyond a critical threshold. This phenomenon has been explained through a balance between two competing effects: the stretching of individual polymer chains and the entanglement of these chains.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset R of its vertices can determine any other vertex uniquely based on its distance to each member of R. A subset of R that does this so is known as a full metric generator, and its smallest possible size is called the full metric dimension of the graph. In this paper, we investigate a variation of this concept called the truncated metric dimension, where we aim to distinguish graph elements with a limited maximum distance, and we aim to determine the smallest size of a subset that does this. Additionally, we provide a new approach to the traditional problem and a specific case where the limited maximum distance equals 2. Furthermore, we provide examples and theoretical constraints on the truncated metric dimension for various graphs.

A machine learning technique, specifically Gaussian Process Regression, has been employed to modify all-sky maps produced by the Fermi-LAT telescope. This technique enhances the visual clarity of the images and adapts to sources with varying intensity over time. When applied to four years of gamma-ray data from 2014, the method outperformed traditional smoothing methods like Gaussian Kernel smoothing, resulting in a 50% reduction in root mean square error. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that training the model using only the source information from the data can enhance the visual clarity of the images. This approach has been showcased through a visual comparison with the all-sky map generated by the Fermi-LAT telescope.

We demonstrate the optimal strategy to achieve a solution in an optimization problem by limiting choices to ranking-based dictatorship or dictatorship based on a randomly selected individual. This approach surpasses other limited decision-making processes, including serial dictatorship, in terms of efficiency. Our findings also reveal the best possible success rate for ranking-based dictatorship to produce an optimal sequence is approximately 0.00004, which is equivalent to 4 in a million chances.

We have developed a method to identify binary asteroids in Pan-STARRS1 images, adapting an existing technique from the Asteroid Binary Telescope (ABT) project. This approach is suitable for detecting binary asteroids in wide-field images captured by the Pan-STARRS1 1.8-meter telescope. By analyzing the detection probabilities of asteroid binaries at various separations and orientation angles, we determined the minimum resolvable separation for detectable binaries in the PS1 data. This finding indicates that we can identify approximately 10 asteroid binaries among 1000 non-grazing contact binaries with periods under one hour. Leveraging the PS1 survey's extensive coverage, we identified a candidate asteroid binary, 2015 TB276, which exhibits a consistent secondary companion across three observations spanning nearly a month. This candidate demonstrates an estimated orbital period of around 10 days, with a semi-major axis of approximately 0.00001 AU.

This research develops econometric methods for inferring relationships in a partially linear regression model, taking into account network data. The model's flexibility is limited by the assumption that unobserved characteristics can be predicted from the endogenous independent variables through a linear regression model. The primary estimation technique employs a two-stage least squares approach, utilizing instrumental variables derived from an instrumenting matrix. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the consistency of the resulting estimator and provides more specific convergence rates for the score function under particular conditions. The paper's methodology is applied to evaluate peer effects in an economic network model, specifically examining the impact of neighbors' alcohol consumption on an individual's alcohol consumption, using data from the National Alcohol Survey. The findings indicate that the estimated peer effects are statistically significant and align with theoretical predictions. The research also highlights the importance of model specification, as the estimated peer effects vary significantly depending on the chosen alcohol consumption index. The research also explores the limitations of alternative estimation techniques, such as the generalized method of moments and the autoregressive model, and finds that the estimated peer effects are either biased or statistically insignificant. The research also discusses the implications of these findings for policy-making and future studies.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for these operators. Specifically, we obtain a Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order type rule for the Leibniz Rule in this context.

This paper explores the application of a complex adaptive filtering algorithm to resolve a class of problems in wireless communications, specifically systems that modulate signals in space. We develop a mathematical model for such a system and derive an update equation for the proposed algorithm, subsequently using this model to analyze and determine the maximum and mean square errors associated with the algorithm's outputs. These findings provide a basis for employing adaptive filtering in scenarios where an optimal receiver is impractical, exemplified in a scenario involving multiple access channels.

We have developed an open-source suite of web-based visualization tools tailored for spectroscopic imaging data, which can be easily customized and adapted for other types of data. These web-based tools offer a user-friendly interface that enables seamless integration with Jupyter notebooks and a variety of programming languages, such as Python, R, and JavaScript. To demonstrate the versatility of our software, we have created two distinct interfaces, which can be accessed at https://spectral-visualization-tools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/. We believe that this open-source software will be a valuable resource for researchers across multiple disciplines, and we have kindly offered to include it as a utility in the forthcoming version 2.0 of the SCExAO/DPS3Ex spectroscopic system.

The South Atlantic rift system, which spans from the Atlantic Central Ridge to the Walvis Ridge, is characterized by a complex geometry and varying orientations. This region is divided into three distinct segments, each with its own opening direction. The Central Atlantic Ridge and the Gulf of Guinea exhibit a north-south orientation, while the Cape Verde fracture zone marks a transition to an east-west direction. The rift system also features numerous transform faults and is marked by significant seismic activity. The Central Atlantic Ridge and the Gulf of Guinea are relatively stable, while the Cape Verde fracture zone is highly active. The South Atlantic rift system is believed to be a result of the interaction between mantle plumes and the African plate, which is undergoing significant deformation. The Cape Verde plume, which is located beneath the plate, is believed to be responsible for the east-west direction of the rift system. The plate is also undergoing significant bending and tilting, which is evident in the seismic activity observed in the region. The South Atlantic rift system is a valuable area for studying the interaction between mantle plumes and the plate, which is essential for understanding the dynamics of the Earth's interior.

A well-known information theory principle, information maximization, has been effectively utilized in various practical applications due to its robustness against specific data distribution issues. However, the theoretical foundation of this method's applicability to learning tasks involving high-dimensional inputs and outputs remains unclear. To address this gap, we establish a theoretical framework that demonstrates under certain conditions, optimizing mutual information equivalent to minimizing task-relevant errors. Building upon this framework, we develop an efficient algorithm to implement information maximization using only unlabeled data. Leveraging this data efficiency advantage, we propose a novel self-supervised method for segmenting medical images. By integrating boundary-aware information maximization, our method effectively prevents the spread of noise present in weakly labeled data. Experimental results on multiple public benchmarks show that our method achieves optimal performance with no training labels and surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods using only weakly labeled data.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how conversational agents can lead and communicate effectively with humans, particularly within the context of Dungeons and Dragons. This study explores whether a virtual Dungeon Master can successfully guide a player through a game, considering their knowledge of the game world and the player's personality. A virtual Dungeon Master is trained using a large dataset of real D&D games and can also learn during a specific game. Our findings show that the virtual Dungeon Master can engage in meaningful conversations, guide the player, and adapt their behavior to achieve these goals. The virtual Dungeon Master's performance can be improved by incorporating theory-of-mind reasoning, which allows it to understand and predict the thoughts of the player. The G4C dataset and the G4C framework are made available to the research community.

Despite significant progress in Natural Language Processing, many NLP systems still rely on traditional machine learning techniques and a large number of pre-processed, manually annotated datasets. One of the pressing challenges in contemporary NLP research is developing robust methods for identifying shifts in word meanings over time using vast amounts of corpora. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a straightforward yet effective approach for pinpointing instances of semantic change by leveraging large-scale language corpora. Our method is designed to be computationally efficient, requiring minimal time to execute. We evaluate our approach on several well-known datasets and also demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying changes in the Oxford English Dictionary. Our results show our method outperforms existing techniques on several of these datasets. Moreover, our approach surpasses human performance in identifying changes in the OED, according to the F1 score.

We propose a new set of functions that depend on $k_\perp$ and are related to partons with a specific transverse momentum. These functions can be derived from twisted gluon and quark distribution functions, which in turn are related to specific correlators of quarks/gluons. We derive the equations that these functions follow, which are influenced by the gluon splitting process $g\to qq$ and the quark splitting process $g\to gg$. These equations are derived using the collinear factorization theorem.

The complex folding process of knotted proteins is not well understood, and their folded structures contain knots that require the formation of knotting loops during folding. To investigate the relationship between the knot type and complexity in protein structures, we developed a method to classify the topology of residue connections in protein structures. This method distinguishes the loop complexity and identifies the main loop responsible for knot formation. By applying this method to proteins with different knot types, we discovered that proteins with higher knot complexity often have preformed loops that contribute to their knot structure. In contrast, simpler knotted proteins and unknotted proteins typically fold from an open chain configuration through the formation of small loops. To further explore the relationship between knot complexity and protein folding, we simulated the folding process of an unknotted, a simple knotted, and a complex knotted protein using a lattice model. Our findings indicate that the preformed loops in complex knot proteins facilitate the folding process, while the formation of loops in simpler knot proteins and unknotted proteins can lead to folding frustration. These findings suggest that the complexity of a knot in a protein structure is related to its folding process, and proteins with highly complex knot structures may have preformed loops that contribute to their knot formation.

Researchers are exploring the possibility of early dark energy (EDE) to address the discrepancy between the predicted and observed values of the cosmic microwave background's amplitude. A new study investigates the parameter space of EDE by utilizing the Planck 2018 and Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) data. By applying a statistical method called the profile likelihood, the researchers derive constraints on the key parameters of EDE, specifically its density and the time it takes to cross the universe's horizon at 0.022-0.042 and 0.018-0.037 for 68% and 68% confidence levels, respectively. Furthermore, by incorporating additional datasets from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) and the Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey (DECaLS), the researchers find more constrained parameter space of EDE, with a 68% confidence level of 0.014-0.033. This study also highlights the significance of using the likelihood method to constrain the parameter space of EDE.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. For any complex curve $C$ within the manifold $(T^4,\omega)$, symplectic blowup at a point $p$ located on $C$ yields a new Kaehler form $\omega_E$ on the resulting manifold $(E,\omega_E)$. This paper investigates the relationship between the symplectic mapping class groups $\pi_0\mathrm{Syct}(E,\omega_E)$ and $\pi_0\mathrm{Syct}(T^4,\omega)$ under a specific condition where the size of $C$ exceeds that of the exceptional divisor but is less than a critical threshold determined by the underlying Kaehler structure $(T^4,\omega)$. Under these conditions, a natural map relating these two symplectic mapping class groups is proven to be fully surjective.

We provide a comprehensive proof of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone theorem in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories, utilizing the properties of the conserved charge operator within the canonical (anti)commutation relations (CAR/Fock) algebra framework. This proof is applicable to theories with local interactions and holds for both massive and massless particle sectors. As a consequence, our result enables a full characterization of massless particles in both types of quantum field theories, based on their continuous symmetries and the associated currents. This full description is achieved under the assumption of a nonvanishing order parameter in both situations.

Recent advancements in neural machine translation (NMT) have achieved remarkable success, but NMT systems still struggle with handling word order variations and long-distance dependencies. To address this issue, researchers have turned to data augmentation techniques, specifically using large language models (LLMs) to generate high-quality parallel sentences. Despite their potential, LLM-generated translations require careful consideration due to their tendency to generate inaccurate or low-quality translations. In this paper, we introduce an innovative framework called DISCO, which utilizes a small NMT system to selectively distill high-quality translations, specifically phrasal counterfactuals, from the LLM-generated translations. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which significantly enhances NMT performance compared to various baselines, including using high-quality data from the LLM. Notably, our method yields substantial improvements in both adequacy and coherence metrics, resulting in a 10% increase in adequate sentences and a 15% increase in sentences with high coherence.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and
neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs.

Remote epitaxy is a highly effective method for growing crystalline films, and recent breakthroughs in remote growth have made it possible to produce high-quality layers of graphene on sapphire. These layers serve as ideal substrates for growing other materials via remote epitaxy. Researchers have successfully used graphene-on-sapphire as a template for growing various Heusler materials, utilizing both remote and pinhole growth techniques. In this study, we investigated the epitaxial growth of Mn2VAl on graphene-on-sapphire using a ternary phase diagram to pinpoint the optimal conditions for both methods. We found that while pinhole growth yields thicker films, it also results in more defects and impurities. In contrast, we demonstrated the feasibility of remote growth for obtaining thinner but higher quality films with reduced defects and impurities. Furthermore, we compared the electronic properties of films grown using both techniques, finding that the films with the highest Heusler phase content exhibited the strongest half-metallic character. In addition, we explored the possibility of achieving a new type of epitaxial growth, which we term "sandwich epitaxy," where the film is nucleated at the interface between the substrate and an overlying layer of a third material. We found that this method can be used to grow films with both high thickness and low defect density, and it opens up new possibilities for engineering the properties of complex multilayer systems.

A code is called $ \Lambda $-linear if it derives from a $ \Lambda $-matrix code, code constructed from a $\Lambda$-matrix. In this paper, we investigate the rank and kernel size of codes based on generator matrices from the ring $ R = \Z_p \Z_{p^2} $, where $ p $ is an odd prime number and $ \Lambda = \Z_p \Z_{p^2} $. We first establish the relationship between code rank, kernel size, and dimension of a code. Next, we establish conditions for codes to be maximum rank distance (MRD) or maximum kernel size distance (MKSD). Finally, we provide examples of MR codes and codes that are maximum kernel size distant.

A novel approach is proposed to determine the ideal gradient of polymer concentration as polymer slugs are gradually blended into a follow-up polymer solution, with the primary focus being on minimizing the viscosity variations experienced by the displacement fluid. The problem is mathematically formulated using a continuous model, with an optimal solution found through a parameterization-based method, and key factors such as polymer molecular weight, flow conditions, and concentration are analyzed through numerical simulations to illustrate the benefits of optimal concentration gradients over traditional methods.

Conditional GANs have achieved remarkable success in image segmentation tasks due to their ability to utilize abundant unlabeled data and a small set of single-label samples.  However, their effectiveness is significantly hindered when dealing with object classes that have irregular shapes, occlusions, or wide variations.  Such classes typically require training on multi-label data, which is often difficult and expensive to obtain.  In this paper, we investigate the possibility of transferring unconditional CyclesGANs to conditionally trained models capable of learning from data with only single-label annotations.  Experimental evaluations on the MS-COCO dataset demonstrate that our proposed method, called MUCoGAN, outperforms traditional unconditional training and other conditional approaches in terms of Dice scores.  Furthermore, our results show that CycleGAN pre-training provides a notable improvement in performance.

This study investigates the property of energy dissipation for a class of time-fractional phase-field equations, specifically those with Caputo time-derivatives of order $\alpha$ where $0<\alpha<1$. We establish an upper bound for the classical energy functional that exponentially decreases over time as $\rho e^{-kt^{\alpha}}$, with $\rho$ and $k$ being positive constants. This upper bound is derived based on the semi-group behavior of the time-fractional operator. Furthermore, this upper bound converges to analogous bounds for both the integer-order heat equation and the porous medium equation when $\alpha=1$.

A well-known result establishes that every pair of compatible observables in a finite-dimensional quantum system corresponds to a pair of commuting self-adjoint operators within a Hilbert space. Our primary achievement is to categorically define the concepts of 'quantum system', 'observable', and 'commuting observable', along with the relationship between them, thereby enabling the demonstration that any such observable can be realized as a self-adjoint operator in a Hilbert space. Furthermore, this process can be reversed to recreate an entire quantum system. We also provide a simplified, explicit formula for the underlying structure known as a 'progenerator'.

The central engines of active galaxies are believed to be powered by accretion onto supermassive black holes, and a magnetic disk known as a magnetically arrested disk (MAD) is considered a likely source of high-energy gamma-rays. These disks produce strong magnetic fields that can accelerate charged particles, and this study aims to explore the gamma-ray emissions from MADs in nearby radio galaxies. Using observations from the Fermi-LAT satellite, we found that the gamma-ray spectra of these galaxies can be described by a power law with a photon index of approximately 2.1, and the gamma-ray emissions are correlated with the radio emissions of these galaxies. The gamma-ray emissions are also consistent with hadronic interactions between protons and gamma-rays produced by the MAD, and this study provides constraints on the characteristics of high-energy cosmic rays in the galaxy's halo. The gamma-ray emissions from these galaxies may also be influenced by the presence of neutral hydrogen gas in the galaxy's halo, and this study provides constraints on the properties of this gas. The gamma-ray emissions from these galaxies may also be influenced by the presence of molecular gas in the galaxy's halo, and this study provides constraints on the properties of this gas. The gamma-ray emissions from these galaxies may also be influenced by the presence of ionized gas in the galaxy's halo, and this study provides constraints on the properties of this gas. The gamma-ray emissions from these galaxies may also be influenced by the presence of dust in the galaxy's halo

This research proposes an advanced statistical model that leverages advanced computational techniques to analyze the cross-sectional distribution of portfolio returns. By leveraging this model, we can evaluate a wide range of portfolio selection methods, including various approaches to optimizing the mean-variance framework. Our results demonstrate that this methodology offers significant computational efficiency and can be applied to large-scale datasets, enabling a deeper understanding of portfolio performance and risk management.

Deep learning techniques have been effective in diagnosing heart conditions non-invasively through phonocardiogram analysis. However, these methods struggle with normal sound processing in the presence of background noise. To address this issue, a novel deep learning architecture has been developed that incorporates two components: a noise reduction module and a sound event detection module. This model utilizes a group normalization-based UNet to learn robust feature representations and employs a specially designed UNet block to capture local patterns in heart sound signals. Experimental results demonstrate that this model outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in noisy environments, achieving a 98.9% F1 score in a six-class dataset and a 97.1% F1 score in a three-class dataset.

The rapid growth of mobile and wearable technology has significantly boosted their use in healthcare, with these devices capable of collecting valuable health data and providing real-time monitoring and alerts. Mobile and wearable technologies enable patients to actively participate in their own care, reducing the need for frequent in-person visits and improving overall treatment efficiency. However, there are significant obstacles to overcome in order to fully realize their potential in healthcare settings. One major challenge is the scarcity of labeled data, which can hinder the development of effective machine learning models. To address this issue, researchers have proposed transfer learning approaches, which involve using a pre-trained model on a data-rich source domain to improve performance on a data-poor target domain. Despite their initial success, these models often require the aggregation of data, which raises serious privacy concerns. To tackle this issue, federated transfer learning approaches have been developed, which enable the transfer of knowledge across multiple devices without the need to share data. In this study, we present a novel federated transfer learning framework that leverages a pre-trained model on a data-rich source domain to improve performance on a data-poor target domain, while simultaneously enabling the transfer of knowledge across multiple wearable devices. Our approach is specifically designed for real-world healthcare settings and incorporates a federated averaging algorithm to update the model iteratively. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in improving model performance on target domains with limited labeled data. Overall, our research paves the way for the development of more effective and secure machine learning models

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher-order moments, including skewness and kurtosis, into a specific framework. Various research areas have explored the use of higher-order moments in portfolio selection, yet a comprehensive review is still lacking. To address this gap, we examine multiple optimization approaches and highlight their interconnections, ultimately providing a unified perspective on how skewness and kurtosis fit into the broader portfolio selection landscape.

We employ a quantum gravity approach to tackle the cosmological coincidence problem, 
focusing on the entropy of four-dimensional de Sitter space. Through an analysis of de Sitter 
tunneling paths, an entropy formula is derived that incorporates de Sitter microstates, 
encompassing both Kaluza-Klein and string theory modes. String theory modes are found to 
significantly influence de Sitter entropy, with the entropy scaling as $e^{\sqrt{M_{\rm Pl}^4/V}}$, 
where $V$ is the compactification scale. This implies that the current expansion of the universe 
is accompanied by a very low energy density within its extra dimensions, with an estimated 
probability of $10^{-10}$ of remaining low for more than a Hubble time.

This paper presents an automated system designed to minimize human intervention in processing applications for a specific program. The system utilizes advanced technologies, including Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP), to extract and update applicant information from various sources such as email, online forms, and spreadsheets. By implementing this system, the agency can efficiently handle a large number of applications and ensure that all applicants are considered fairly. Unfortunately, the available data for predicting application approval is limited, which hampers the development of such predictive models.

This study addresses a complex control issue in which the cost of transitioning between states can change in a dynamic and unpredictable manner. Specifically, we consider a setting where the costs can vary in a non-smooth and erratic manner over time. The problem is particularly challenging due to its connection with a type of partial differential equation that exhibits discontinuities in both its time and spatial components, as well as its classification as an optimal stopping problem with moving boundaries. To overcome these obstacles, we develop a novel approach to solve the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Isaacs quasi-variational inequality, thereby obtaining a solution representation and a method for numerical approximation. The proposed approach is then applied to a specific scenario involving the management of inventory in the presence of fluctuating prices.

To explore potential sources of lepton flavor violation, we examine the significance of rare decays arising from asymmetric leptoquark pair production in proton-proton collisions. As an illustration, we focus on the scenario where leptoquarks $D$ and $D'$ possess distinct masses and interact solely with first-generation quarks and second-generation quarks and leptons. In this context, we investigate the production of $D D'$ pairs where $D$ decays into a down quark and an electron, while $D'$ decays into a charm quark and a muon neutrino. To assess the sensitivity of such a model to current experiments, we estimate the expected number of non-observation of $D \to e \mu$ decays given the maximum possible cross-section for leptoquark pair production. Furthermore, we consider the implications of this model on the forward physics at the LHC and the potential for detecting long-lived leptoquarks in the Muon Ionization Cooling Experiment at the Future Circular Collider. As a result, we derive constraints on the possible values of leptoquark masses based on the findings of these studies.

Temporal data analysis is crucial for understanding time-dependent processes, but traditional methods often struggle with complex scenarios, such as biological experiments that produce short and high-dimensional time series. These series typically have limited time points but many variables, making them difficult to model using conventional approaches. To address this challenge, we developed a novel supervised learning framework called TimeLearner, which combines multiple machine learning models to improve prediction accuracy. TimeLearner was tested on two biological datasets, including a study on the effects of the antibiotic vancomycin on gene expression and a study on the effects of the drug doxorubicin on cell viability. The results showed that TimeLearner outperformed traditional temporal learning methods, such as Dynamic Time Warping and Hidden Markov Models, in terms of prediction accuracy.

We have developed a new method to determine the electron temperature of the molecular gas in galaxies, based on the concept that their C{\sc i} lines are formed under non-thermal conditions. Our study involved 14 local galaxies with high-resolution data for their carbon monoxide and carbon ci lines. We created electron temperature maps for these galaxies using a new excitation model and found that the average electron temperature in their molecular gas reservoirs is significantly lower than previously estimated, at around 10 K. This revised temperature is comparable to the kinetic temperature of the same reservoirs. The implications of this finding are that galaxy star formation rates and masses derived from carbon ci lines are now more accurate and consistent with those derived from other methods. Additionally, this discovery suggests that the carbon ci lines may be more effective tracers of a galaxy's star formation potential than previously thought.

We tackle the long-standing puzzle of the anomalous flavor anomalies in both $K$ and $B$ mesons by introducing a novel explanation, introducing two types of quarks that belong to different categories but share a common characteristic of vectorlike. These new quarks interact with the Standard Model through both single and double quark exchanges, with the interaction strengths being dictated by the respective quark's composite nature. By simultaneously fitting flavor anomalies and new quark mass measurements, we determine the feasible parameter space for this two-sector model, revealing that this scenario could potentially resolve the flavor anomalies puzzle if the masses of the new quarks are within the range of the Large Hadron Collider's discovery capabilities.

Let $S_n$ be the set of all permutations of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. The distance between two permutations $\pi$ and $\sigma$ in $S_n$ is defined as the number of elements at different positions, denoted as $d(\pi, \sigma)$. A sequence $A = (A_1, \ldots, A_k)$ is considered $r$-separable if for any permutation $\pi$, there exists an index $i$ such that the distance $d(A_i, \pi)$ is less than or equal to $r$. In this study, we determine the minimum sum of distances between each $A_i$ and $\sigma$, denoted as $f(r, n)$, for the case where adjacent elements in the sequence are at a distance of more than $r$. We also determine the optimal sequence $A$ for a specific case where the sequence consists of all possible $(n-1)$-tuples.

Research on using deep learning for instrument identification has primarily focused on classifying samples from a single instrument, with little research on identifying multiple instruments using a single sample. In this study, we explore the potential of a deep neural network to recognize an instrument from a single sample, leveraging a hierarchical structure to enhance the model's ability to transfer knowledge from tasks with more data to tasks with less. We evaluate our approach on the MAIO dataset and find that our hierarchical model outperforms a non-hierarchical counterpart in transferring knowledge from tasks with more data to tasks with less.

Academic researchers who read research papers often seek information by asking questions, a process that drives the pursuit of knowledge. To support this, providing high-quality answers to relevant questions can guide them in further investigation. To facilitate this, we have created a dataset comprising 1,513 questions and their corresponding answers derived from computer science research papers. Notably, 41.1% of these questions are resolved using information contained within the same paper, while 31.1% are answered using details from related papers. By offering this dataset, we aim to assist in developing models capable of anchoring their reasoning within the context of long-form documents. Consequently, this can enhance the capability of these models to support information-seeking tasks.

Researchers are planning to use future pulsar timing arrays to detect gravitational waves from inspiralling eccentric binaries in the Milky Way. To accurately model the signals these arrays will measure, researchers need to incorporate higher-order post-Newtonian terms, specifically up to 2.5PN order. By implementing an analytic method to calculate the Fourier spectrum of these waveform components, the study demonstrates that including 2.5PN order only increases the computation time by a small margin, around 10%.

We analyze the long-term behavior of an asymmetric simple random walk on a one-dimensional integer line, where an infinite number of independent random walks interact through nearest-neighbor particle exchanges. The dynamics of a specific particle, initially at the origin, are examined as the time scale expands infinitely. It has been previously shown that, when considering a finite time period and expanding the time scale significantly, the distribution of the original particle's location follows a specific set of probabilities. In this study, we demonstrate that, for any given time within a finite interval, there exists a sequence of modified starting conditions for the random walks such that, when examining the particle's location at a much larger time scale, the probability of it being at a specific position is nearly the same as under the original starting conditions. Furthermore, we establish that the positions of the original particle at consecutive, closely spaced times correspond to the first instance when the particle's location changes from one position to another.

This paper examines the fundamental mathematical models used to model infectious diseases, with a focus on their application in the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. We discuss various modeling approaches, including stochastic and deterministic models, and explore key parameters such as the basic reproduction number R_0, which is central to understanding the spread of the virus. Additionally, we examine the challenges of estimating these parameters and their implications for public health policy.

We examine the unique characteristics of a Majorana fermion, specifically its particle-particle symmetry, in a system of N independent, non-degenerate Majorana fermions. By analyzing the statistical properties of this fermionic model, we investigate how the Majorana term influences the distribution of occupation numbers, energy, and other quantities. Our study reveals that the distribution of energies of N independent fermions can be expressed as the convolution of N Gaussian distributions, each with varying widths. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in the limit of large N, the energy distribution becomes a Gaussian with a width that scales as the inverse square root of N. Notably, in this scenario, the fermionic system exhibits behavior similar to a bosonic system in the large N limit.

Acronyms are prevalent in the digital age, yet they pose comprehension challenges for non-native speakers, individuals with language difficulties, and automated systems. This issue is particularly pronounced in low-resource languages, which significantly hinders the effectiveness of Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. To address this problem, existing methods for acronym resolution in well-documented languages have been developed, but a comprehensive approach for the broader scope of language is still lacking. We introduce an innovative, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation system, which we term MadDog, that is capable of identifying and providing a range of meanings for acronyms across any language. MadDog is user-friendly and user-friendly, providing a user-friendly interface for users to input acronyms and receive a range of meanings for the same. MadDog is capable of processing any acronym, regardless of its language, and provides a user-friendly interface for users to input acronyms and receive a range of meanings for the same.
