We have theoretically analyzed the process of converting a spinor atom pair into a bosonic molecule through a process known as association, which involves a specific light-induced three-body process. This process occurs when two atoms in the same spin state absorb a photon and form a molecule in its ground state. Our study reveals that this association process is limited by a specific rate which can be altered by adjusting the frequency of the applied light. This rate is significantly influenced by a factor known as the scattering length, which can be used to either enhance or inhibit the three-body recombination process. As a result, we demonstrate that it is possible to control the maximum number of molecules that can be produced from an initial cloud of atoms.

DNA storage technology offers a cost-effective and high-capacity data storage solution, yet its primary limitation lies in the difficulty of updating data. A novel encoding scheme has been developed to address this issue by enabling data to be organized in a hierarchical format and updated with minimal regeneration. In this approach, data is divided into updateable chunks arranged in a tree-like structure, with each node containing a unique DNA address and relevant information. When updating data, only the affected nodes need to be regenerated, with changes propagating up the tree. A specific algorithm has been proposed to facilitate this process by enabling parallel node regeneration and minimizing the required DNA operations. Experimental results have demonstrated the system's efficiency in terms of operation count, processing time, and storage usage.

Topological insulators and semimetals are characterized by exotic properties resulting from nodal lines, which are one-dimensional points of zero energy gap within the momentum space. These nodes can be classified by a non-trivial integer invariant, ensuring the stability of the nodal line against perturbations. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of mathematical frameworks used to describe this topology, specifically focusing on symmetry classes that allow only unitary symmetry. Various models are presented to illustrate the origins of these topological features, which can be described using a single Hermitian matrix with a unique symmetry property. This work also highlights recent experimental and theoretical advancements in systems that exhibit nodal lines, which are not protected by unitary symmetry alone. These include photonic crystals, mechanical metamaterials, and electrical circuits.

A brain tumor is a serious condition that affects the nervous system and can be categorized into two types: benign and malignant.  Statistics show that approximately 4.5 million people are affected by brain tumors each year, with a significant number of these cases being fatal.  Due to the complex nature of tumors, distinguishing between benign and malignant types is a significant challenge.  Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a widely used imaging technique for diagnosing brain tumors, as it is non-invasive and provides detailed images of the brain.  However, MRI images can be difficult to interpret, especially when it comes to identifying and segmenting tumors.  Researchers are using deep learning techniques to analyze MRI scans and classify brain tumors, with some of these models being trained on large datasets of MRI scans.  In this paper, we propose a novel multi-task attention guided network that uses MRI scans to classify and segment brain tumors.  Our network is designed to tackle the interdependence of these tasks by using a multi-task attention mechanism.  We conducted extensive experiments on two widely used MRI datasets, and our results show that our network outperforms other state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy and efficiency.  We believe our approach can contribute to the early detection and diagnosis of brain tumors, which is crucial for improving patient outcomes.

Differentiable rendering systems have gained popularity in solving inverse problems due to their ability to accurately model complex scenes. However, traditional differentiable renderers often struggle with high computational costs, particularly when dealing with real-time data. This issue arises from the use of volumetric methods, which require solving an enormous number of linear equations. An alternative approach using surface-based methods can significantly speed up computation, but has been limited by the inability to model certain effects, such as global illumination. This limitation is addressed by a novel framework that combines both methods in a single, unified system. The hybrid system leverages volume-based methods to model light transport and a differentiable shadow map to handle occlusion, resulting in a more efficient and accurate solution. By utilizing this system, researchers can solve inverse problems with real-time data, as demonstrated in experiments with both synthetic and real-world datasets.

A cutting-edge deep learning method for restoring high-speed videos from low-resolution interlaced footage has been developed.  Our approach utilizes multiple convolutional neural networks to track moving patterns in real-time and fills in missing information, allowing for smooth video restoration at 60 frames per second using GPU technology.  We have created two datasets for testing, including modified versions of Bikes and Traffic from the HMDB50 collection, and measured our system's performance against top methods for both offline and real-time video restoration.  The source code for our algorithm is publicly available.

The investigation focuses on the neutron distribution within nuclei, specifically examining the root mean square radii of neutron distributions in both neutron-rich and isotopic nuclei using a non-relativistic mean field model and a covariant density functional theory. A detailed comparison is made with experimental data obtained from recent measurements at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams. The study reveals that the radius of neutron skin in isotopes is accurately predicted by the new theory, whereas it overestimates the value in neutron-rich nuclei by approximately 0.02-0.04 fm. The investigation highlights the significance of spin-orbit terms in describing the nuclear mean field and the impact of the nuclear basis on the calculated results. The study also reveals the correlation between the radius of the neutron distribution and the moment of inertia of the nucleus's rotational states.

A significant challenge in numerical weather prediction is accurately and efficiently calculating numerical weather forecasts. This study presents an innovative approach to numerical data assimilation, which combines a deep learning-based fast solver for atmospheric dynamics with a limited-depth water equations model. This combined model is used to forecast the development of mesoscale coastal currents and tropical cyclones. The results show that the proposed model can accurately forecast the mesoscale coastal currents and tropical cyclones, outperforming traditional numerical models in certain scenarios. The results also indicate that the proposed model has the potential to be applied to operational numerical weather forecasting.

HDR photography combines multiple images taken at different exposure levels to overcome limitations of a single image. The smartphone camera's automatic exposure setting, however, makes bracing difficult due to its ability to adapt to the scene's brightness. This research evaluates the effectiveness of various methods to control the camera's automatic exposure setting, including the use of exposure fusion and a custom-designed exposure bracketing approach. The results demonstrate that exposing the images by 2 to 3 stops of underexposure yields the best outcome when using exposure fusion on a smartphone. The developed methods are evaluated through user testing and subjective assessments.

Causal deep learning is an emerging field that combines causal inference with deep learning, yet there is a lack of comprehensive information about its fundamental concepts, key methodologies, and practical applications. This review aims to provide a causal framework for understanding machine learning, outline the primary structures used to model causal relationships, and discuss the connection between these models and machine learning algorithms. It also explores the benefits of incorporating causal knowledge into machine learning models, particularly in improving their performance and reducing biases. In addition, this review covers causal representation learning, representation learning from interventional data, and representation pretraining, and it offers a roadmap for future research in causal representation learning.

Understanding temperature variations within industrial reactors is crucial for enhancing their efficiency and safety. However, measuring temperature in real-time and in three dimensions is a challenging task. In this study, we demonstrate the use of non-invasive, 3D temperature mapping with real-time imaging capabilities through rapid magnetic resonance imaging. By utilizing this technique, we can visualize temperature distributions in a fixed bed reactor in three dimensions and in real-time. Our findings show that the temperature profiles obtained through imaging align with temperature measurements taken using thermocouples. Furthermore, we found that temperature variations within the fixed bed are not uniform, with significant differences observed in both the vertical and horizontal directions. These temperature variations are influenced by several factors, including the type of gas, gas flow rate, heating power, and the size of the particles. Our study provides valuable insights into the temperature distribution within a fixed bed reactor, which can inform the design and optimization of industrial processes.

This paper provides a simplified proof of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which follows from the recent breakthrough by Cumming-Hamidi-Mahowald on the $b$-principle's weakness. Cumming's work relies on the established result of Habegger regarding the virtual homotopy equivalence of $\overline{M_g}$ and $\overline{K(g)}$. Additionally, this study incorporates a discussion on the Madsen-Weiss theorem's connection to the virtual homotopy equivalence of $\overline{M_g}$ and $\overline{K(g)}$.

This research compares various multilevel multigrid methods for solving the equations of cardiac mechanics. We examine different solution techniques for the resulting system of equations, including iterative solvers like the conjugate gradient method and its restarted variant, as well as direct solvers based on the minimum residual method and Gaussian elimination. By comparing these approaches, we can determine the most suitable method for solving the complex equations of cardiac mechanics. Furthermore, we can use this knowledge to create an efficient and accurate simulation tool for cardiac mechanics that can be used to study the effects of heart disease and to design better medical treatments.

The standard semicircle and circular laws for random matrices rely on complex unitary matrix ensembles, where matrix entries are not independent. In contrast, this paper explores the broader scenario of independent entries, utilizing a recently developed framework based on the asymptotic behavior of permutations. The authors establish new results for the variance scaling of random matrices, showing convergence to specific variance-driven distribution laws for certain factorial-dependent variances, and showing that the standard laws are a subset of these findings.

Persuasive multimedia, particularly video, has a powerful impact on conveying complex concepts and influencing public opinion. The rapid development of AI technology has significantly accelerated the creation of complex multimedia content, leading to advancements in AI-powered persuasive image and video production. This paper provides the first comprehensive survey of AI-powered persuasive multimedia, with a specific focus on persuasive video generation. We categorize AI-powered persuasive video generation methods into three main classes: emotion-driven, style transfer, and cross-domain generation, examining the underlying principles, representative models, and applications of each approach. Additionally, we discuss the unique challenges and potential future directions of AI-powered persuasive video generation. This survey not only highlights the current state of the field but also offers valuable insights for researchers and practitioners in this area. The accompanying website (https://neuroaizhang.github.io/SPCv2022/) provides a visual overview of AI-powered persuasive video generation techniques.

This paper introduces the concept of False Sense of Security (FSS) in cross-domain dialogue systems, which occurs when users are misled into believing the system genuinely understands them due to overly confident responses, despite the conversation being essentially a one-way interaction. To address this issue, we have developed an evaluation metric called Measuring the False Sense of Security (MFSS). This metric is designed to quantify the extent to which users experience FSS during conversations with dialogue systems. MFSS is calculated by comparing the difficulty of distinguishing secure from non-secure sentences between current and ideal sentences. The ideal sentences are those that users can easily distinguish from secure sentences, thereby indicating a lower FSS experience. To demonstrate the effectiveness of MFSS, we conducted an empirical study with 30 participants on a restaurant recommendation dialogue system. The results showed that the system's users did experience FSS, with a difference of 0.4 bits in sentence distinguishability. The MFSS score can guide dialogue system developers in creating more transparent and honest systems that openly communicate their limited understanding and domain-specific nature.

To achieve high-performance acoustic metamaterials in the ultrasonic range, novel approaches are being developed to circumvent the size limitations imposed by wavelength on conventional methods. A new class of structures known as metagratings has been introduced, which, despite their periodic nature, can interact with waves smaller than a single wavelength. These microacoustic metagratings, with a lattice size of 100 micrometers, have been fabricated using two-photon lithography and demonstrated an extraordinary 18-dB transmission gain at 425 kHz. A theoretical model has been developed to explain their performance, which can be tailored to minimize unwanted diffraction effects. This advancement paves the way for miniaturized, high-frequency acoustic devices with improved sensitivity.

Standard Brownian diffusion occurs when a particle's displacement follows a Gaussian distribution, but some studies have observed anomalous diffusion with non-Gaussian probability distributions. This study focuses on one-dimensional diffusion and uses a non-invasive method to track individual particle trajectories, which are found to exhibit power-law tails. The mean squared displacement grows linearly with time, yet the typical displacement grows at a slower rate. It is demonstrated that this type of anomalous diffusion can be explained by the random variation of the diffusion coefficient over time, and the model's parameters are derived from the observed trajectories. Furthermore, the study finds that the distribution of diffusion coefficients is universal and independent of the particle or experimental method used.

A comprehensive mathematical framework is developed to model linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between optical resonators and waveguides. The theory is designed to be applicable to a wide range of systems, including those exhibiting linear coupling, self-Kerr effects, and cross-Kerr nonlinearity. By deriving general expressions for mode frequencies and mode shifts, the model provides a detailed understanding of system behavior. The simplicity of the mathematical formulation enables explicit solutions for mode frequencies in various configurations, facilitating direct comparison with experimental data. The model's versatility is demonstrated through the analysis of linear coupling, self-Kerr effects, cross-Kerr nonlinearity, and systems with competing linear and Kerr couplings. The theoretical framework is further applied to investigate mode hybridization in coupled resonator systems, yielding insights into resonance anti-crossing behavior. The model's predictive capabilities are illustrated through the analysis of a coupled waveguide-resonator system, where the model accurately predicts observed anti-crossing behavior in experiments. The research is supported by funding from the National Science Foundation and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

This paper builds upon established connections between stability, reachability, and controllability of control systems, extending previous results that relied on a bounded control domain. Our analysis shifts focus to control systems with unbounded controls, and our primary findings provide conditions for such systems to be controllable, have a reachable set with specific properties, and exhibit asymptotic controllability, thereby drawing parallels to control systems used in robotics.

A deep learning method has been developed to generate highly detailed images from low-resolution images, specifically tailored for a type of fluid flow at a rectangular boundary. A type of neural network, known as a generative adversarial network, has been trained to create a model that maps from low-resolution images to high-resolution images, and has been validated through multiple tests. The model's performance was evaluated by comparing reconstructed images to images obtained from direct numerical simulations, and the model's accuracy was also assessed at different levels of Reynolds number. Furthermore, key features of the flow, such as the size and location of low-speed regions, were analyzed to assess the model's ability to capture these features accurately. The study also examined the stability of these features over time and found that the model's predictions were consistent with the statistical behavior of the flow. The model's accuracy was also evaluated in terms of the mean squared error, and it was found that the model's performance was optimal at a certain level of Reynolds number. The model's ability to capture the flow's behavior was also assessed in terms of the distribution of the low-speed regions, and it was found that the model's predictions were consistent with the distribution obtained from direct numerical simulations. The model's ability to capture the flow's behavior was also assessed in terms of the correlation between the low-speed regions, and it was found that the model's predictions were consistent with the correlation obtained from direct numerical simulations. The paper addresses the absence of a classical wave equation for non-relativistic quantum particles and suggests that the Schrödinger equation, which describes the wave function, should be viewed as the appropriate wave equation. A key argument presented is that the probability current, which is related to the wave function, must be conserved, and this conservation can only be achieved if the time-dependent part of the probability current satisfies the same mathematical requirements as a conserved charge in electromagnetism. This leads to the conclusion that the time-dependent part of the probability current must satisfy the wave equation. Additionally, the paper examines the behavior of bound states and shows that they would not exist if the time-dependent part of the probability current did not satisfy the same conditions as the electromagnetic vector potential. This further reinforces the argument that the probability amplitude, which is the square root of the probability density, should be interpreted as a physical field, and this interpretation is consistent with the Bohmian mechanics.

Deep neural networks excel at solving complex tasks, but their reliability is compromised when they encounter novel, unseen data. This limitation is addressed by enhancing their confidence calibration to accurately reflect open-world uncertainty. This paper proposes a new approach to quantify open-world uncertainty using an energy-based function, which is derived from the model's energy landscape. This function is then integrated into an energy-based uncertainty model that updates the model's output probabilities. This approach is unique in its ability to capture open-world uncertainty. To validate this approach, we utilize the Open-Set Recognition benchmark, which measures a model's confidence when encountering unseen data. This validation demonstrates the superiority of our proposed method over existing techniques. Furthermore, we show that this method is applicable to any classifier and can be trained with minimal labeled data. This paper also introduces a new data augmentation technique to improve the model's performance on rare classes. This is achieved by creating synthetic samples that mimic the energy landscape of unseen data. This approach is shown to be effective in improving the model's accuracy and confidence calibration.

To test the effectiveness of reinforcement learning algorithms in complex, ever-changing scenarios, researchers have developed evaluation frameworks. However, these frameworks lack support for environments that continuously evolve over time. This paper introduces Lifelong2, a new assessment framework where the agent is tasked with mastering a series of environments that gradually change, without any information about the future environments. As a result, reinforcement learning agents in these environments face the challenge of lifelong learning. We also provide evaluation frameworks for both lifelong and myopic approaches, and our experiments show that the proposed assessment framework can be used to evaluate reinforcement learning agents in dynamic, evolving scenarios.

Modern businesses are increasingly adopting process automation technologies to enhance efficiency and productivity. However, as the complexity of processes grows, identifying and documenting them becomes a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel approach to process identification and documentation based on data streams. This approach involves monitoring processes in real-time through stream-based analysis, pinpointing recurring patterns, and automatically generating a declarative process model using a bottom-up method. To validate our approach, we employ a well-known discovery algorithm and demonstrate its effectiveness through a case study.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, the transition from localized to conducting states is well-documented, but in photonic quasicrystals, local interactions can lead to unexpected outcomes. A shift from conducting to isolated states is observed in photonic quasicrystals, which we investigate using a model and experimental data. By altering the coherence of light in a fiber-based experiment, we observe this transition from conducting to isolated states, confirming our theoretical predictions.

Liger, a new generation infrared camera for the W. M. Keck Observatory, is set to revolutionize observations in the spectral range of 0.8 to 2.4 micrometers. It is capable of delivering 25000 images per second with 2048x2048 pixel resolution, utilizing the Keck's adaptive optics system. To process and analyze the vast amount of data generated by Liger, a powerful data processing system has been designed and built. This system, known as the Data Reduction System, is designed to process up to 1.5 terabytes of data per night, utilizing 120 terabytes of storage and 24 CPU cores. To facilitate the analysis of the data, Liger has been equipped with a range of software tools, including the Data Acquisition System, a data visualization tool, and interfaces with the Astropy and PyRAF software packages.

To overcome the diffraction limit, we propose a new approach that utilizes spatial mode multiplexing and demultiplexing techniques. This method allows for the transfer of a bio-object's fine details onto a larger scale, effectively increasing its apparent resolution. By employing demultiplexers made from spatial light modulators, we show that a binary object with a specific size can be imaged with significantly improved clarity. The results indicate that the resolution achieved through this technique is solely dependent on the characteristics of the bio-object, rather than the imaging system. The theoretical framework is validated through numerical simulations.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

The ecosystem's stability is often influenced by sudden shifts in the population of key species, which can have far-reaching effects. Understanding the early warning signs of these population changes is crucial for effective conservation and management. A mathematical model is used to explore how specific species interact within an ecosystem and identify the early indicators of significant population shifts. The model reveals that the rate of change in the population of one species can be used to predict the upcoming transition in the ecosystem. Additionally, the model shows that the early warning signs are closely related to the timescale of interactions between the two species. This discovery has important implications for the development of early warning systems in the ecosystem.

To determine the role of stellar bulges in shaping the global star formation properties of a galaxy population, we focused on separating galaxies by their morphological type. Using a bulge-to-disc decomposition method, we estimated the properties of each component for a sample of 10,000 galaxies from the COSMOS-LEDA database. By doing so, we were able to compare the star formation rates of bulge-dominated and disc-dominated galaxies, and found that the average star formation rate of bulge-dominated galaxies is lower than that of disc-dominated galaxies, with the difference increasing with stellar mass. This result suggests that the presence of a stellar bulge is a key factor in limiting the star formation rate of a galaxy. Furthermore, we found that the star formation rates of bulge-dominated galaxies are lower than those of disc-dominated galaxies, with the difference increasing with stellar mass. This result suggests that the presence of a stellar bulge is a key factor in limiting the star formation rate of a galaxy.

This paper introduces a multi-task learning approach to sentiment analysis across different languages, utilizing a shared neural network architecture.
Our method leverages a single set of sentiment classification layers, combined with language-specific embedding layers, to perform sentiment analysis on both English and German texts.
By training the network on datasets from both languages, our model learns to transfer knowledge between languages and effectively handles sentiment classification tasks.
Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms individual single-language models, achieving superior performance in sentiment analysis across both languages.

We examine the impact of removing or downgrading self-invalidating and self-upgrading fence instructions on fence-based synchronization. Our analysis indicates that eliminating self-invalidating fence instructions from a subset of cores in a multiprocessor system can lead to observable fencing violations. Similarly, upgrading self-invalidating fences to self-downgrading fences without corresponding memory barrier adjustments can also result in fencing violations. We have experimentally validated these findings using a system with variable fence configurations and a downgrading Intel Xeon processor, demonstrating that eliminating or inverting fence instructions can cause unexpected program order issues. Our research provides a comprehensive set of guidelines for developers to anticipate and manage the effects of changing fence instructions on system behavior.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem posits that if integers 'a' and 'b' within a set 'A' have a sumset 'A+A' of size at least 2k, then there exist arithmetic progressions 'P_a' and 'P_b' of sizes at least k, such that the sum of their elements contains at least 2k-4 elements. This requirement can be relaxed to 2k-3, where 'P_a' and 'P_b' need only have at least k-1 distinct sum elements. This paper aims to prove this revised condition.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst parameter $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $A^{H}_{t}$ be an independent symmetric $\alpha$-stable motion in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with characteristic exponent $\alpha > 0$. This paper provides conditions under which the image of the fractional Brownian motion with deterministic drift $B^{H}+f$ has positive Lebesgue measure and an interior that is not empty, as well as an absolute continuity result for the semigroup generated by these processes. Additionally, it is shown that the measure of the image of the stable motion with deterministic drift is always full, as is the measure of the Skorokhod embedding of these processes.

To investigate quantum chaos within the Henon-Heiles model, we apply Dirac's time-dependent variational principle and the Gutzwiller approximation, utilizing JK wave functions. Our results indicate that while these functions accurately represent regular states, they fail to capture the complex structure of the quantum chaotic sea.

X-ray image analysis has been widely used in diagnosing various diseases, and during the COVID-19 pandemic, radiologists have heavily relied on this method for detecting and assessing COVID-19 cases.  Despite numerous studies being conducted to aid radiologists in making accurate diagnoses, there is still a lack of understanding regarding the underlying characteristics of COVID-19 abnormalities in X-ray images.  This study aims to shed light on the potential features that may be associated with ICU admission in COVID-19 patients, by utilizing deep learning techniques to analyze images and extract relevant features.  Our approach involves a comparative study of images from three groups of patients: those who required ICU treatment, those who did not, and healthy individuals.  Through our experiments, we were able to identify specific regions in images that exhibited significant differences in terms of texture and intensity, and these regions were found to be primarily located in the upper left and right areas of the images.  Our findings suggest that ICU admission may be associated with a decrease in lung volume, as well as the presence of specific patterns such as consolidation, ground-glass opacities, and air bronchograms.  To further validate our results, we employed a range of statistical tests and visualisation techniques, and these methods allowed us to identify the most influential features that differentiate between the three groups of patients.  Our study contributes to the broader understanding of lung diseases and may provide valuable insights for the development of more accurate and interpretable image analysis techniques

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.

This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the current status of Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) systems. A thorough examination of the dataset and the identified false positives in the system's predictions reveals a significant issue: the models struggle to accurately identify spatial relationships. A key limitation of existing methods is their reliance on object detection and classification alone, without incorporating image captioning techniques. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that leverages long-short term memory (LSTM) networks to learn the spatial relationships between objects and generates descriptive sentences to filter out the false positives. Our proposed method is evaluated on the Visual Genome dataset, where our results show a significant improvement in the mean average precision for the VRD task.

This study introduces an innovative action recognition framework that excels in low-light conditions with a minimal dataset. The framework combines a pre-trained action recognition model with a small, well-lit dataset to generate a robust representation of actions in low-light conditions. A key component of the framework is the Delta Sampling R-BERT module, which efficiently transfers knowledge from the well-lit dataset to the model by fine-tuning a small portion of the pre-trained model's parameters. The framework utilizes the transfer learning approach to minimize the impact of low-light conditions on the action recognition model. The results demonstrate that the framework outperforms other methods in low-light action recognition benchmarks, achieving superior performance with a minimal dataset.

This report outlines the design and implementation of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor (CAPP) on a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). Unlike traditional von Neumann architectures, CAPP employs a novel architecture that utilizes parallel processing and eliminates the von Neumann bottleneck. The design features a unique content-tagged data format and a set of instructions designed to manipulate data directly within the memory. A specific CAPP prototype was developed using a Xilinx Zynq-7000 SoC FPGA, which integrates an ARM processor and an FPGA fabric. This prototype demonstrates a 10x speedup in matrix multiplication compared to a von Neumann architecture with similar resource allocation. The results suggest that CAPP has the potential to provide high-performance computing capabilities for a wide range of applications.

We have identified a galaxy at redshift 3.08 within a massive group, located 0.61 megaparsecs from the group center. This galaxy is part of a large system that includes a massive group and a galaxy group, and it exhibits a quiescent, lopsided disk with a mass of 1.4 times 10 to the 10th power solar masses. Inside this galaxy, we have detected a compact, centrally located bulge with a mass of 2.5 times 10 to the 9th power solar masses. Using a combination of integral field spectroscopy and spatially resolved spectroscopy, we have determined that the galaxy's disk is rotating at a speed of 200 kilometers per second, and its gas is being accreted from the galaxy's center at a rate of 1.5 solar masses per year. We have also found that the galaxy's star formation is occurring at a rate of 1.3 solar masses per year, and that its gas is enriched with alpha elements at a level of [alpha/Fe] = +0.35. These findings suggest that the galaxy is undergoing a transformation from a disk galaxy to a bulge-dominated galaxy, and that this transformation is being driven by the accretion of gas and the formation of stars. We have conducted a comprehensive examination of the Universal Texture Zero Flavour model, which offers an analytical approach to obtaining the mass and mixing patterns observed in nature. This model is supported by our advanced numerical analysis, utilizing an efficient algorithm based on Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods to estimate the likelihood of various model parameters. The resulting parameter space is then presented through a combination of statistical intervals and 3D likelihood surfaces, providing a robust foundation for future experimental validation at facilities such as the muon collider. Furthermore, our analysis yields a significant prediction for the rare process of $B_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$, which will be tested in upcoming experiments at the LHC and potentially observed with higher precision at a muon collider.

This study examines a specific nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, where N is 5 or greater. We establish the existence of a periodic family of solutions that exhibit a localized behavior, as well as their uniqueness within each periodic interval. Furthermore, we derive a quantitative relationship describing how these solutions change. Our proof techniques involve combining variational methods with infinite dimensional mountain pass arguments, as well as an infinite dimensional version of the Nehari manifold approach. Notably, this work is the first to apply the Nehari manifold method to an elliptic equation featuring a localized behavior.

Current state-of-the-art neural program generators still struggle with accuracy and efficiency, often producing solutions that require extensive editing to meet quality standards. Additionally, they lack the capability to guarantee correctness, forcing reliance on time-consuming human code review. In this study, we introduce a novel approach that combines neural program generation with static analysis to simultaneously enhance solution quality and correctness. By using a static analysis tool as a guide during generation, our approach enables the model to learn the syntax and semantics of the target language more effectively. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the classic code completion problem, where we achieve a significant improvement in solution quality and correctness compared to the baseline. Furthermore, we provide a code change suggestion example that showcases the benefits of our approach.

A solar flare that occurred on November 7, 2004, was observed in the 1-8 Angstrom wavelength range with a GOES X-ray flux of 1.03E-09 W/m^2. This event was accompanied by the release of 1.4E-09 neutrons per square centimeter per second per steradian, with an energy greater than 100 MeV. A simulation of this event using the FLR code revealed that 1.1E-09 solar neutrons would decay into 6.3E-09 solar protons with an energy greater than 20 MeV. A comparison of simulated and observed data from the PAMERA satellite showed that the number of detected particles was consistent with the simulation, confirming the existence of neutron decay protons.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations, taking into account both shear and bulk viscosity. Next, we compared our theoretical predictions to the results of the Boltzmann equation, using a 14-moment approximation. This allowed us to establish the connection between kinetic theory and relativistic hydrodynamics. Our analysis revealed that the real and imaginary components of the dispersion relations for shear modes are accurately described by the theory, whereas viscous scalar modes exhibit discrepancies. Specifically, the scalar mode's imaginary component is inaccurately represented by a factor of $2$ in the relationship between the imaginary component and the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio. This discrepancy is attributed to the inclusion of an unphysical mode in the 14-moment approximation. To rectify this issue, we propose a modification to the approximation that eliminates the unphysical mode. This revised approximation yields the correct imaginary component of the dispersion relation for scalar modes. Our findings also indicate that the unphysical mode's influence on the shear modes is minimal, as it only affects the imaginary component of the dispersion relation by approximately $10\%$. This minor discrepancy is consistent with the inherent limitation of the 14-moment approximation.

One effective technique for detecting anomalies in time-series data is using deep learning methods like LSTM and GRU, which have been extensively researched and applied. However, these traditional models require significant storage and computational resources, making them impractical for edge devices that need to process data in real-time without access to historical information. Although some lightweight models have been developed, they still rely on access to past measurements and cannot easily adapt to new data without retraining. To address these challenges, we propose InQMAD, an innovative approach for real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurement, which can be easily trained on historical data and continuously adapted to new data through quantum measurement. Our method leverages a simple linear model and a memory-efficient update process, making it an ideal approach for resource-constrained environments that need to monitor time-series data in real-time. Our experiments demonstrate that InQMAD outperforms state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy and efficiency, while using significantly less memory and computational resources.

Recent court decisions in the US have sparked debate over the extent to which the government can compel the creation of new security measures. This issue has been particularly contentious in the context of the case between the government and Apple, where Apple was ordered to create a custom software tool to bypass Apple's security measures on an iPhone. In this paper, we take a different approach by examining the concept of compulsion from the perspective of a user who is already in possession of the key. We propose a new security model called "Don't Trust--Verify" (DTV) that allows a user to entrust a third party with the creation of a custom software tool, while still being able to confirm that the tool operates within acceptable parameters. We then demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by presenting a secure protocol for the iPhone case, where the user can be assured that the government's software tool will not be used to access other data on the device.

We have developed a comprehensive model that simulates the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution process. This model is versatile and can be applied to various real-world quantum hardware systems, taking into account the unique characteristics of each system. The model is designed to be user-friendly and can be easily customized to meet specific project requirements. It is implemented in Python and is freely accessible on GitHub.

We develop an approximate constant-factor solution for a specific CSP problem, which is PTAS when the number of variables significantly exceeds the number of constraints, assuming the instance is sparse. This result is achieved without any restrictions on the cost function or the problem's structure. Moreover, our solution is a more efficient version of an existing algorithm, which was previously shown to be EPTAS for sparse instances by Chuzhoy et al. in 2020, thereby improving their result. Notably, our approach is randomized and relies on the technique of conditional rounding, which was first introduced in the context of CSPs by Bansal in 2010. This technique allows us to bypass a key barrier, which was first identified by Goemans in 2005, which was that conditional rounding was not suitable for solving optimization problems. This was the first time this barrier was overcome in the context of CSPs.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The proposed method utilizes a Lagrange-Galerkin approach, which is the first of its kind to achieve high-order accuracy for this specific type of equation. The scheme's stability and convergence properties are mathematically proven, and its ability to accurately model complex systems is demonstrated through its application to Lagrangian mean field games. The results are visually supported by numerical experiments.

Recent experimental data from $B$ meson decays to charged hadrons and tau leptons have been successfully explained by the $U_1$ leptoquark model. This model's simplicity and consistency with $SU(2)$ gauge symmetry make it a compelling theory. In this study, we examine how $b \to c$ decay data can be utilized to forecast the rare decay of $\Lambda_b \to p \tau \bar{\nu}$ within the $U_1$ leptoquark model. Our theoretical predictions for $\Lambda_b \to p \tau \bar{\nu}$ are found to be in good agreement with experimental observations. Additionally, we calculate the direct CP asymmetry in this decay, which is predicted to be around $10^{-3}$, a value that is too small to be detected by current experiments.

Advancements in machine learning and neural networks have achieved remarkable success in solving complex classification and regression problems. Despite their widespread adoption, the underlying decision-making processes of these models remain elusive, hindering their application in high-stakes fields such as medicine and law. This paper delves into the challenges of interpreting deep neural networks and reviews various visualization techniques and explanation methods developed to address this challenge. By examining these approaches, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of current visualization and explanation methods for deep neural networks. Furthermore, we discuss the limitations of existing techniques and identify potential avenues for future research.

Observations of solar-like stars reveal a surprising increase in their spin rates as they age, which contradicts theoretical predictions. Current models suggest that stars should spin down more rapidly over time, but the observed increase in angular momentum transport on the solar surface is not fully understood. To investigate this phenomenon, we analyzed the rotation rates of 1100 G-dwarf stars and found that the observed angular momentum transport on the solar surface is within the normal range for stars of its age. However, the results also indicate that the Sun's rotation rate is unusually fast compared to other stars of its mass and age. The study also reveals that the observed rotation rates of G-dwarf stars are influenced by their metal content, which may be due to the effects of convective overshooting. The implications of these findings for the evolution of the Sun and other stars are discussed, and the study suggests that the observed effects on the solar surface may be due to the ingestion of planets.

The escalating spread of misinformation on social media poses significant challenges, particularly when it combines emotional appeals with deceptive content. Although current methods for detecting such news have achieved notable success, they are constrained by their reliance on manually annotated training data. In contrast, this study introduces a novel approach that utilizes emergent training to create a model capable of detecting fake news across multiple modalities. Our meta learning-based framework, the Meta Neural Process Networks (MNPNs), enables the model to generalize to unseen data by merging three distinct networks and training them jointly to process input content, images, and user metadata. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art single and multimodal techniques, particularly in detecting socially engineered fake news.

This study examines the one-dimensional transport equation with a periodic boundary condition, 
$\partial_t u + v \partial_x u = \partial_v^2  u$, where the velocity $v$ follows a parabolic distribution 
$V$ on the interval $[-1,1]$. The initial condition is given by a Dirac delta function $\delta(x)$ at $t=0$. 
The research reveals that the support of the solution's density expands over time, 
and the velocity support is described by a set of curves that are generated by the flow of the transport 
equation. Notably, the solution's behavior is further analyzed, including the impact of initial conditions.

This paper investigates the impact of packet loss on a discrete time status updating system. We analyze the age of information under the First-Come-First-Served policy, specifically when service times follow an exponential distribution. We derive the probability generating function for the sojourn time of update packets and, through its properties, obtain the mean and variance of the sojourn time distribution. We then express the expected age of information in terms of the probability generating function of the sojourn time distribution. We also derive an explicit formula for the mean sojourn time and use it to obtain the mean age of information. We also consider the M/G/1/1 queue and derive the Laplace transform of the sojourn time distribution, obtaining the mean age of information in terms of this transform. We also derive an explicit formula for the mean sojourn time distribution and use it to obtain the mean age of information. We provide numerical examples to illustrate the effects of update packet loss on the age of information.

This study delves into various quantum algebras, specifically quasi-bialgebras, that arise from set-theoretic solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation. Given a set-theoretic solution $r: A\times A\to A\times A$ of the Yang-Baxter equation, we define an associated algebra structure $(A,r_\ast(A)\times r_\ast(A),1_A)$, where $1_A$ is the identity element of the algebra $A$. The investigation focuses on the property of this associated structure being a quasi-bialgebra. Notably, we establish conditions under which this associated structure exhibits a deeper algebraic characteristic, that of a weakly associative-triple algebra. This condition is met when the set-theoretic solution $r$ satisfies a more complex equation, the super-Yang-Baxter equation. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between this condition and the existence of a compatible pre-Lie algebra structure on $A$. We provide sufficient conditions for the occurrence of this pre-Lie algebra structure, focusing on certain types of set-theoretic solutions $r$.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices (GCMs) have been the subject of significant interest due to their potential applications in massive MIMO systems. Building on this, researchers have now taken the next step by exploring Golay complementary arrays (GCAs) to address capacity limitations in large-scale systems. Although GCAs were initially proposed over a decade ago, the scarcity of novel construction methods has hindered their practical implementation. This paper presents four new GCA construction techniques, including two methods for generating real-valued GCAs and two methods for producing complex-valued GCAs. The dimensions and dimensions difference of the constructed GCAs are also highlighted in a comparative table for clarity.

Quantum interference in silicon-based scanning tunneling microscopy has been observed in both spin-resolved and non-spin-resolved modes. A non-trivial oscillation pattern in the spin signal was identified, which we attribute to the interference between two electron waves with different symmetries located in the valley moir\'e pattern's high-symmetry points. A tight-binding model successfully simulated this phenomenon. Furthermore, we found that atomic-scale spin exchange can be manipulated by controlling the overlap between the two interfering electron waves, as demonstrated by our use of silicon monosilane. This provides a means to create quantum states of silicon-based carbon isotopes that possess both valley and spin degrees of freedom.

Complex systems are characterized by their intricate relationships and dynamic behavior, which are often difficult to understand. A significant challenge in studying these systems lies in the limited availability of data, which is typically collected in the form of time series. This limitation hinders the application of graph-based methods that are commonly used for analyzing complex systems. In this study, we address this challenge by developing a novel graph-based approach that utilizes mutual information to map the relationships between system components. This approach is then used in conjunction with a graph neural network to model the dynamic behavior of the system. A significant advantage of this approach is its ability to leverage the strengths of both methods, which allows for the accurate modeling of complex systems even in the face of limited data. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we apply it to a variety of systems, which include the Lorenz attractor, the Mackey-Glass system, and several biological and social systems. Our results show that this approach outperforms existing methods in a range of performance metrics, which include mean squared error, coefficient of determination, and coefficient of correlation.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have significant applications in algebraic topology, particularly in determining the structures of homotopy groups for spheres at $p$-adic levels. Our newly developed counting principles and recursive counting methods will be utilized to refine previously established partial structures on spheres at $p$-adic levels and establish new relationships between spheres and certain formal group laws.

A cutting-edge deep learning technique known as semantic segmentation has achieved remarkable success in identifying and identifying tumors within medical images. To enhance the accuracy of this method, researchers have employed a large dataset for training, but such extensive data collection is often impractical. To overcome this data limitation, a novel approach has been proposed to generate synthetic images containing various types of tumors using an improved version of the adversarial variational auto-encoder, resulting in a new framework called Brain Lesion Synthesis via Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder. This framework generates a diverse range of tumors, including meningiomas, gliomas, and pituitary adenomas, and has been demonstrated to produce high-quality results that closely resemble real images. The generated synthetic images have also been utilized to train the semantic segmentation model, and the results show significant improvement in model performance compared to using only real images for training.

Strong quantum nonlocality, a form of impossible local hidden variable model, is demonstrated for measurement-assembla-based realism using an unextendible product basis state of two qubits under specific projective measurements. This type of quantum state, where no set of product states can be added without becoming entangled, is shown to exhibit strong quantum nonlocality when two such states are combined in an uncorrelated manner. The research also identifies the minimum number of states required in an UPB to achieve this quantum nonlocality, which is four states.

The Complete Safe Coordination Algorithm (CSCA) is a novel method for synchronizing the movements of multiple robots to complete a task without any collisions. The CSCA builds upon the concept of safe trajectories by incorporating the time dimension to generate paths that guarantee safety. To evaluate the effectiveness of this algorithm, we conducted experiments using a pair of AstroBots, a type of programmable robot, to map and navigate through the corridors of the SDSS-V Science Tunnel. The results of these experiments demonstrate the CSC's ability to coordinate the robots' movements to complete the task in the most efficient manner possible. The CSCA algorithm is also being utilized in other projects, including the SDSS-V Science Tunnel, to ensure the safety of the robots working in close proximity to each other.

GP 2 is a graph-based programming language designed for efficient implementations on GPUs, building upon the foundation of GP. To address performance limitations, GP 2 incorporates several key enhancements, including memory management optimizations, a high-performance graph format, and a technique for minimizing memory usage. GP 2 also boasts a sophisticated compiler, integrating features such as a code generator, an instruction format, and a method for efficient memory usage. To demonstrate the capabilities of GP 2, the compiler was applied to a range of graph algorithms, including connected components, minimum spanning trees, graph coloring, and graph isomorphism. Experimental results indicate that GP 2 outperforms GP and existing graph algorithms on GPUs, with the compiler producing optimized codes that execute up to 10 times faster than existing GP implementations.

A versatile image analysis technique is now being developed to address the limitations of task-specific models. These models, while achieving high performance, are costly to create and deploy due to the need for extensive, task-specific training. In contrast, a unified framework is emerging that utilizes a single neural network to extract features applicable to various downstream tasks. By leveraging contrastive learning, this unified framework effectively learns a shared embedding space that preserves both local and global data structures. Experimental results on multiple datasets and tasks, including task compatibility, feature selection, clustering, and outlier detection, demonstrate the superior performance of contrastive learning over other methods, including unsupervised techniques.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Praeger and Saxl in 1984.

Working with categorical data in machine learning models is complicated by the need to learn parameters for each category, which can be numerous. This issue is particularly pronounced in models with sparsity-inducing penalties, as they often struggle with variable selection in high-dimensional categorical datasets. In this paper, we introduce an improved version of the Group Lasso model, which is commonly used for categorical data, and develop an efficient and stable optimization method. Our approach is backed by theoretical guarantees, and our results in experiments show significant performance gains over existing methods, including up to a hundred-fold reduction in computational time.

Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance on numerous tasks, surpassing human levels in many areas. However, these models' training processes remain largely based on unstructured information, such as Wikipedia articles and Common Crawl data. In contrast, modern structured databases contain extensive and high-quality knowledge that is systematically organized, yet is seldom utilized in large-scale training processes. To bridge this knowledge gap, we present a new method called SKI (Knowledge from Structured Knowledge Infusion into LLMs), which takes a unique approach to infusing Wikipedia and MS-Excel into LLMs. Our experiments show that LLMs trained with this method outperform models trained solely on unstructured data in various tasks, including natural language inference, commonsense reasoning, and math problem-solving. Furthermore, we demonstrate that pre-trained LLMs can be effectively fine-tuned with this new knowledge infusion method, achieving significant performance gains on multiple benchmarks.

This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$, and investigates their behavior as they approach both local and nonlocal extremes. As the interaction range $\delta$ narrows, these models converge to standard diffusion models; conversely, as it broadens, they approach a fractional $s$-diffusion model, with $s$ directly related to $\delta$. However, existing nonlocal models either fail to provide clear insights into their relationship with both limits or require significant adjustments to achieve convergence to the fractional limit. To overcome this limitation, the authors introduce a revised nonlocal model that maintains convergence to both limits with minimal transformation, allowing for a smooth transition from standard to fractional diffusion based on the interaction range.

When it comes to panoramic photography, the images are usually captured with the camera aligned vertically. This paper proposes solving this problem by leveraging the known direction of gravity to minimize the number of required images. By utilizing this prior knowledge, we can determine a set of rotations that place all images on a common horizontal plane, assuming the images are rectilinear. This problem can be formulated as a minimalist approach, and we develop an efficient solution by leveraging the geometric properties of SO(3) rotations. The result is a set of discrete solutions, from which the optimal one is selected based on the highest probability. Experiments demonstrate that our method produces high-quality panoramic images with a high degree of accuracy.

This research paper delves into the pole cancellation mechanism of an Eisenstein series associated with $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. A primary objective is to outline the removal of a specific pole at $s_0=\frac{n-1}{2}$, composed of an irreducible cuspidal component $M_0$. A secondary objective is to characterize combinatorial structures of sets defined by partial Podleski integrals, integral equations, and local factors that contribute to the pole's cancellation. A key theorem establishes a bijection between these sets and the collection of all partitions of the set $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$. Furthermore, a new method is proposed to determine the order of the pole's order, based on a newly defined quantity $\gamma(P)$ associated with each partition $P$. The paper also provides an explicit formula for the local factor at the prime $p$ at $s_0$, and a numerical example is given for the case when $n=4$.

Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that significantly impairs motor control and affects a vast number of individuals worldwide. Despite its widespread impact, motor control deficits in Parkinson's disease are not fully understood, hindering the development of effective treatments. To address this knowledge gap, researchers have turned to computational modeling to simulate and predict how the brain's neural circuits function in Parkinson's disease. However, existing models often lack the necessary detail to accurately replicate the complex changes observed in the basal ganglia of Parkinson's disease patients. In this study, we present a novel computational model of Parkinson's disease that incorporates a detailed representation of the basal ganglia, including its cell types and neurotransmitters. Utilizing electrophysiological data from healthy and Parkinson's disease-affected marmoset monkeys, we developed a biophysically realistic model of the basal ganglia that mimics the changes observed in marmoset brains affected by Parkinson's disease. Our model successfully replicates the abnormal oscillatory activity and altered firing patterns observed in marmoset brains affected by Parkinson's disease, providing a detailed understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying motor control deficits in this condition. This model may pave the way for more effective treatments for Parkinson's disease by providing researchers with a detailed platform to test and develop new therapies.

A high-quality line rendering is crucial for creating an engaging and easy-to-read map, and it is particularly important to achieve anti-aliasing on line joins. However, existing anti-aliasing techniques often struggle with performance, especially when rendering complex maps with numerous lines. In this research, we aim to develop an anti-aliasing method that maintains a high frame rate while rendering line joins. We propose a technique that leverages the GPU's overdraw capabilities to generate frame-rate friendly anti-aliasing effects. Our evaluation shows that this technique outperforms current anti-aliasing methods, delivering visually appealing results and a high frame rate of 60fps. As an example, we have created a line rendering library that utilizes this technique, and it is available for download on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenJiaxuan/LineJoinAntiAliasing.

We utilized the KOOLS-IFU on the Seimei Telescope to conduct integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located at redshifts less than 0.04. These galaxies are situated in a merging system and are among the most luminous in the universe. Our observations covered a wavelength range of 0.85-1.65 $\mu$m, allowing us to obtain spatially-resolved spectra of H$\alpha$, [NII]6584, [SII]6718,6731, H$\beta$, and OIII5007. Our data revealed a variety of star formation rates and specific emission line ratios, which we compared to a comprehensive dataset of 1000 galaxies. Our results suggest that galaxies with high infrared luminosity and a compact structure are more likely to have a quenched star formation process. Our results also suggest that galaxies with a merging structure are more likely to have a quenched star formation process. Our results also suggest that galaxies with a high gas fraction and high gas surface density are more likely to have a quenched star formation process. Our results also suggest that galaxies with a high mass and a high mass-to-light ratio are more likely to have a quenched star formation process.
